name: Niccolò de Franceschi
text: The earliest man the Croatian branch counts as its own. He acted for Guillaume Grimoard — later Pope Urban V — in negotiations between Louis I of Anjou and the Republic of Venice. By a charter given at Buda on 8 March 1359 Louis received him into the hereditary Hungarian-Croatian nobility with arms, for estates around Zadar. Every Zadar and Omiš descent traces to him.
note: The family no longer holds the charter; the claim rests on the Croatian nobiliary literature and on the 1838 submission to the Austrian commission.

name: Toma de Franceschi
text: Notary of Zadar, and the man who keeps the Croatian branch's noble claim from being only a story about a charter. He was admitted to the city council of Zadar by hereditary right and swore the oath in **1714**; he was appointed **public notary in 1722**, and he held the office for a full forty years. The detail worth having is what language he worked in: he ran his practice in **«Illyrian» — Croatian — as well as in Italian**, in a city where the notarial record is otherwise Latin and Venetian. His son **Ivan Krševan** followed him into the same office. In **1838** the family submitted its documentation and genealogy to the Austrian commission on nobility, and was admitted to the register of the Dalmatian nobility printed by Heyer von Rosenfeld in 1873.
note: Not kin — the Zadar–Omiš house, not the Carnian one this archive follows. He is here because the old family site carried the Croatian nobiliary account of that house in full and this archive had never named him; and because a notary of forty years leaves an archive. The Zadar notarial fond is the obvious place to test everything the nobiliary literature says about this family. Hrvatski biografski leksikon, vol. 4 (Čoralić, 1989), p. 353.

name: Andrea dei Franceschi
text: Grand Chancellor of the Republic of Venice from 1529 until his death in 1551 — the highest office a man not of the patriciate could hold, the permanent head of the chancery under the elected Doges. He was Titian's friend, and Titian put him into the «Presentation of the Virgin» now in the Accademia. He owned two portraits of himself by the painter. The head in both derives from Titian's own portrait now in the Detroit Institute of Arts. A double portrait at Hampton Court, in the Royal Collection, was cleaned in 1958 and gave up a third figure that had been painted out at some point — it is now Andrea, Titian and another man. A further portrait is in the National Gallery of Art at Washington, where the gallery's own catalogue declines to call it Titian: the handling is harsher and cruder, the colour less subtly modulated.
note: Not kin, and this archive has never claimed him. He is of the Venetian de' Franceschi, and the family this site follows is a Carnian one that reaches Istria about 1700. He is here because he is the reason the surname is in every art-historical index, and because for a year the roadmap carried «Andrea and Titian» as an unfinished item. It is finished.

name: Piero della Francesca
text: Born Piero di Benedetto, son of Benedetto de' Franceschi, a tradesman of the Tuscan Franceschi. He is called after his mother — la Francesca, as she was known by marriage into the family — and he is the reason the name is in every history of the Renaissance. The Urbino diptych puts Federico da Montefeltro and Battista Sforza in profile against a continuous landscape, and puts perspective at the service of two faces.
note: The name is the same name. Whether the Tuscan Franceschi and the Friulian-Istrian De Franceschi share an ancestor is not shown by anything in this archive, and the surname is far too common to assume it.

name: Francesco de' Franceschi, the painter
text: A Venetian painter of the middle fifteenth century whose birth and death dates are simply not known — «active 1443 to 1468» is as close as the record gets, which is itself a fact about how the trade was recorded. He painted religious work on church commission. The style follows Michele Giambono, and he may have worked alongside Antonio Vivarini. An altarpiece of 1447, most likely from a church in Padua or Venice, is attributed to him and hangs in the Museo Civico at Padua; two panels — a St Mary Magdalen and a St Catherine of Alexandria — are in the Ashmolean at Oxford; a St Michael the Archangel and a series on St Mamas are also given to him. **And he can now be looked at.** Two of the pictures named here are online and out of copyright: the Ashmolean's *St Mary Magdalen* and *St Catherine of Alexandria*, both bought for Oxford in 1850, and both narrow gold-ground panels from a dismembered altarpiece — you can see the saw-cuts in the composition. A *Martirio di San Mamante* is at the Museo Correr in Venice, and Yale holds two more scenes of the same saint's legend. Five surviving fragments of one lost story, in three countries.
note: Not kin. A fifteenth-century Venetian, two and a half centuries before this family reaches Istria. He is here because the roadmap has carried him as unfinished since before this archive had a roadmap, and because an item does not stop being owed by being ignored.

name: Piero, as the sixteenth century drew him
text: Vasari's Lives gave each artist a woodcut portrait in an ornamental frame. Vasari, who came from Arezzo where Piero's frescoes are, complained that Piero's pupil had taken the credit for his master's books — which is the reason we know Piero wrote them.

name: Girolamo de' Franceschi
text: Born at Capodistria into a family from Udine — the Friulian origin again — the son of Pietro di Tommaso, he entered the Servites as a boy, professed in 1472, took his doctorate in theology at Bologna in 1474, and was four times vicar general of the reformed Congregation. Appointed bishop of Corone in Greece on 18 February 1496, he never went: the see fell to the Turks in 1499, he resigned it in 1502, and he stayed with his patrons, first Cardinal Giovanni Michiel and then Cardinal Domenico Grimani, Patriarch of Aquileia, in whose household he moved towards Friuli. He died at Udine in 1513 and was buried on 12 August in the family tomb. Catholic-Hierarchy adds that he was an auxiliary bishop of Aquileia from 1510 and was buried at Venice; the Dizionario Biografico has neither (it records only that the historian Paschini guessed he became a canon of Aquileia, with no document), so those two are left out here.
note: Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, vol. 49 (1997), by Matteo Sanfilippo, citing Paschini, «Fra' G. de F. servita e vescovo di Corone», Studi storici sull'Ordine dei Servi di Maria II (1934), pp. 3–13, and Eubel, Hierarchia catholica II, p. 138 (provision 18 Feb 1496, annate book Obligationes et Solutiones 83). Catholic-Hierarchy, bishop/bfrancgi. No descent from or to this archive's lines is claimed.

name: Francesco Franceschi
text: A printer who worked in metal rather than wood, which is why his 1565 Orlando Furioso — an engraving before every canto, an engraved frame round every argument — was copied by English publishers a generation later. He also printed music, including Zarlino. Two probable relatives, Giovanni Antonio de' Franceschi at Palermo and Venice and Giacomo Franceschi of Venice, printed music too. His imprint survives on the shelf as well as in the catalogues: the Biblioteca Estense at Modena holds his 1565 Venice edition of **Leon Battista Alberti's «L'architettura»**, printed «per Francesco de' Franceschi» — five years before another press of the name put out Palladio.
note: **Siena, not the Regina house (18 Nov 2026):** [Lastraioli 2012](https://books.openedition.org/enc/531?lang=en) has Francesco de' Franceschi of **Siena** settling in Venice in the late 1560s, printing learned vernacular works, with his sons **Zaccaria, Giovanni Antonio and Giacomo** keeping a shop «al segno della Pace» in San Zulian; the article keeps him apart from Domenico and Pietro's house, and names a Francesco of Padua (c. 1582) and a Girolamo of Siena, bookseller in Florence, as other men of the name. The "probable relatives" above are, on that article, his sons.

name: Domenico de' Franceschi
text:
**He printed Palladio.** In 1570 the press of Domenico de' Franceschi at Venice issued Andrea Palladio's «I quattro libri dell'architettura» — the four books that taught Europe and then America how to build, and the single most influential architectural book ever printed. Inigo Jones's annotated copy is the founding document of English classicism; Jefferson built Monticello out of it. The title page carries the imprint «In Venetia, Appresso Dominico de' Franceschi, 1570».

Another Venetian press under the name. He published the woodcut procession of Süleyman the Magnificent going to the mosque (1563), Charles V's storming of La Goletta near Tunis, and a Battle of Lepanto printed in the year after the battle — news engraving, sold in the street while it was still news. He also published a Battle of Lepanto in the year after the battle — news engraving, sold in the street while it was still news.
note: A Goleta sheet is at the Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen. No connection to this family is claimed or known; the press is here because it is the largest thing anyone of the name ever put into the world. **What a study of the house adds (18 Nov 2026, `doc` for what the article says; the registers not seen):** [Lastraioli 2012](https://books.openedition.org/enc/531?lang=en) (École des chartes, *Passeurs de textes*, pp. 75-98) has him founding the press «al segno della Regina» in the Frezzaria in 1557, working with his brother **Pietro**, and dead about 1574 (so Brusegan); some authors make him a Brescian, the article does not decide. The Inquisition summoned him on 8 July 1558 over two bawdy *historie* and named him among the printers called on 1 December 1571 (Archivio di Stato di Venezia, Santo Uffizio, b. 156, fasc. 1, fol. 35). **Pietro** ran the house to about 1576 (summoned 31 October 1573 and named on 21 March 1573, same fascicle, fol. 49v); then heirs: **Bernardino** (signed at least six editions with mark Z1204, still printing in 1587), **Prospero** (directing 1591-93) and **Pietro junior** (directing 1594-97, dead 30 January 1597), after which Girolamo Foglietti, Pietro junior's brother-in-law, took the sign. The clerks wrote the name *Domenico de' Franceschi*, *Domenego di Franceschi* and, in Latin, *Dominicum de' Francisci*. The article says plainly that this house is **not** that of Francesco de' Franceschi of Siena.

name: Alessandro de Franceschi OP
text: Bishop of Forlì from 1594. His father was Hananel — Nello — Graziadio da Foligno, a rabbi who on baptism took the name Alessandro Franceschi in homage to Cardinal Alessandro Farnese. The surname in this instance is not descent but conversion: a name chosen, not inherited.

name: Mariano de Franceschi
text: Trained at the Accademia di San Luca and under the Spaniard Baldomero Galofre; debuted at the Amatori e Cultori exhibition in Rome in 1876 with a still life, then turned to landscape and genre. He exhibited at Turin in 1884, at Capri and Rome in 1888, and at Venice.

name: Carlo De Franceschi
text: Born at Moncalvo di Pisino — Gologorica — son of Giuseppe, a smallholder loyal to Austria, and Lambertina Peschle of Volosca. Schooled by the parish priest, then Pazin, Fiume and the seminary at Gorizia; law at Graz, where his anti-Austrian views hardened. He wrote L'Istria: note storiche, and he wrote the letter to Giovanni Kobler that this archive leans on for the family's own account of itself. The Blasonario Giuliano's entry for his family calls him «uno dei più arditi patrioti istriani» — one of the boldest of Istrian patriots — and records that he was Secretary of the Provincial Assembly of Istria.
note: He is this family's historian, and the one who says the family came from Carnia about 1700. He also buried at least four children — see the register of the dead. And he is still cited: Egidio Ivetic writes that for medieval Istria one must rely on Benussi, Carlo De Franceschi and De Vergottini.

name: Camillo De Franceschi
text: Carlo's youngest child, and the one who turned the family's history-writing into a profession. Archivist and historian of Venezia Giulia; he edited the statutes of Labin, the chartulary of Piran, and the study of the Castropola lordship over Pula, and wrote the «Storia documentata della Contea di Pisino» — the documented history of the county his own family lived in — published posthumously in 1964 by his son Carlo. He died an exile at Venice in 1953. The armorial notes him as Commendatore and past President of the Società Istriana di Archeologia e Storia Patria.
note: Still standard. A 2021 doctoral dissertation on Venetian Istria names three figures who «tower» over the field — Bernardo Benussi, Giovanni de Vergottini and Camillo de Franceschi — and quotes Egidio Ivetic that for medieval Istria «ci dobbiamo affidare agli studi di Bernardo Benussi, Carlo De Franceschi e Giovanni De Vergottini»: we have to rely on them. Father and son are both named. And more than standard: the same dissertation notes that Camillo used primary sources «today unavailable due to the detrimental effect of the Second World War and its bloody aftermath in Istria». For some documents his articles are now the only witness. Josip Banić, «Venetian Istria in the Embrace of a Nascent Dominium», CEU 2021.

name: Giovanni — il Zuane — de Franceschi
text: In the Venetian-Ottoman war of 1718 he led volunteers from Piska by way of Vrulja to the siege of Imotski, joined after three days by German and Swiss mercenaries with cannon and horsemen from Sinj. Imotski and Vrgorac were taken and the Dalmatian-Bosnian border was fixed where it still runs. The Republic gave him the estates of Arch-bey Čaušević — land, houses, a mill, a tower on the Vrljika. Kačić-Miošić put the feat in a song.
note: An old family tomb with carved arms stands before the altar of the church at Piska.

name: Giovanni de Franceschi
text: Professor, historian, essayist, travel writer; chancellor to the bishop and honorary canon of Split. He published the monthly La Dalmazia at Zadar and argued in it for an enlightened cosmopolitanism. His poem Dalmatinska vila appeared in 1844.

name: Jean-Marie-Antoine Defrance
text: Écuyer to the Emperor, brigadier general, made a count of the Empire by letters patent of 2 July 1808 at Bayonne. His arms: party azure and gules, cut argent — azure with the sign of the military counts; gules with a golden cock; argent with three azure halberd-irons, two and one. His portrait was engraved by **Claude-Marie-François Dien after Henri-François Riesener** in 1820.
note: A separate line: the French Defrance, not the Istrian Defranceschi. Included because the surname converges.

name: Jean-Baptiste-Marie Franceschi
text: Brigadier general and aide-de-camp to the King of Spain and the Indies, made a baron of the Empire by letters patent of 23 June 1810. The Corsican Franceschi came from Florence: a Taddeo Franceschi crossed to Corsica early in the fourteenth century, and his descendants served Genoa until Corsica went to France in 1768.
note: **Two generals, and one of them is not this entry (18 Nov 2026).** The text above (aide-de-camp to the King of Spain, the portrait) describes **Jean-Baptiste-Marie Franceschi-Delonne**, a general of brigade who served on King Joseph's staff and died at Cartagena on 23 October 1810 (Wikipedia, `lore` for us; no birthplace given there, other sources say Lyon 1767). A **different** general, **Jean-Baptiste, baron Franceschi**, was born at Bastia on 5 December 1766 and died at Danzig in March 1813 (Wikipedia, from the 1911 Britannica; 13 or 19 March); the tree has him as *Jean Baptiste Marie Cristophe De Franceschi*. The Malta genealogy list of the Empire's nobility ([no. 622](https://maltagenealogy.com/french-empire-1/)) prints «Franceschi, Jean-Baptiste-Marie, Baron de l'empire 23 June 1810, (1775 Lyon – 1813 Dantzig)»: a Lyon birth that belongs to the one man and a Danzig death that belongs to the other, with the patent date this entry gives to the Spain man. **Which of them the letters patent of 23 June 1810 name is unsettled**; neither Wikipedia article gives a date. A Paris notary's inventory of Jean-Baptiste Marie «Francisqui, général d…» (MC/ET/XCI/1491, found on the SIV, abstract cut off) may be the Danzig man's, a lead only. No kinship to this family is claimed for either.

name: Marcantonio de Franceschi
text: Secretary of the Council of Ten in 1567 — the same body Andrea de' Franceschi had served as secretary from 1519 before his election to the Grand Chancellorship. Two men of the name, a generation apart, inside the most secret organ of the Venetian state. He belongs to the Candia and Seghetto branch: the armorial names him in the same entry as the four brothers who gave the Republic a hundred thousand ducats in 1716.
note: Blasonario Giuliano, «Franceschi (de) — Seghetto, Capodistria, Umago».

name: Francesco de Franceschi
text: Bishop of Pola from 24 September 1423 until his death in 1426 (the year is uncertain), and before that bishop of Modon (Methone) in Greece, provided on 10 June 1409 and obligated on 12 July 1409; he is called «Franciscus Novello» in the Latin lists and «Novello» is a byname. The earliest office-holder of the name recorded anywhere in Istria, a century before the Chancellor. The Gravisi manuscript's Capodistria family, originally Venetian, aggregated to the nobility of Pola in 1580 and extinct, is the family the Blasonario gives him; no Church record read here names his father or his city, so that link is the manuscript's word, not a document.
note: Catholic-Hierarchy (bishop/bfrancesf), citing Eubel, Hierarchia catholica I, pp. 352 and 404; Eubel I p. 352 (read on the archive.org scan) lists «Franciscus Novello» at Modon, provided 10 June 1409, obligated 12 July 1409. The Pola entry, p. 404, was not found in the scan's text. Blasonario Giuliano, «Franceschi — Capodistria»: that family bore a bent bend charged with a lion passant or.

name: Luca di Nicolò de Franceschi
text: The first of the family whose nobility is actually proved in the registers of the Archive of the Duke of Candia. His father Nicolò was castellan of Castel Milopotamo in 1500. The family had been enrolled in the Cretan nobility earlier than this, but 1488 is where the documents begin — and it is the point at which the Seghetto branch's story stops being tradition and starts being record.
note: Blasonario Giuliano, after Spreti. Everything before 1488 in that family's account of itself — the prefect Feramondo of 474, the flight to Padua, the crossing to Crete between 1211 and 1257 — is tradition.

name: Carlo Prospero Defranceschi
text: Court poet and librettist in the Italian theatres of the Habsburg capitals. He wrote the libretto of Antonio Salieri's «Angiolina, ossia Il matrimonio per sussurro», and styled himself on his title pages «Licenziato de' Dritti» — licensed in law — and «Riducitore del Sacrificio interrotto, e d'Amore e Psiche». His «Il Principe d'Itaca», a dramma eroicomico reduced from the German for the use of the Italian theatre, was staged at the new theatre in Prague in 1797 under Domenico Guardasoni, the impresario who had commissioned «La clemenza di Tito» from Mozart six years earlier in the same house.
note: Two printed libretti carry his name: the Prague «Principe d'Itaca» of 1797, in the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, and the Florence edition of «Angiolina» of 1815, which credits «Libretto by C. P. Defranceschi». No connection to this family is claimed.

name: Ante Defrančeski
text: Born at Ližnjan near Pula on 1 February 1894 — the third-largest concentration of this surname in the whole record sweep. Trained at the Kastav teachers' college in 1912, volunteered for the Salonika front, left Istria when it became Italy, and became a professor at the teachers' training school in Zagreb. He wrote nine books between 1925 and 1940 on how a child learns to read and write — and the Croatian Biographical Lexicon heads his entry with the háček, «Defrančeski».
note: No descent from this family is shown and none is claimed. He is here because he is where the Istrian Defranceschi went when they went the Croatian way.

name: Jean Defranceschi
text: Historian of Corsica and of the French Revolution. His essay «Robespierre et la Corse» stands in the Lille volume «Robespierre: de la Nation artésienne à la République et aux Nations», and argues that the Corsican revolution of 1729–69 — drowned at Ponte Nuovo when Robespierre was eleven — was a live example to the men of 1789, and that Corsica in that year was not yet legally French.
note: A Corsican bearer of the name, and a reminder of how far the patronymic travelled: the family's own map already carries Corsica and a Corsica-to-Genoa marker. No connection to any line on this site.

name: Camillo De Franceschi, in Croatian
text: Camillo's «Storia documentata della Contea di Pisino» — the documented history of the County of Pazin, published posthumously in 1964 — is still the standing authority. Current Croatian scholarship cites it page by page: Elvis Orbanić's study of the bishops of Pićan leans on it a dozen times, and Irma Huić's study of Gračišće opens its bibliography with it. In 2023 it appeared in Croatian as «Povijest Pazinske knežije na temelju isprava», from Josip Turčinović of Pazin.
note: Carlo wrote the history of the province; his son wrote the history of the county; and the county's history is now in the language of the people who live there. It can be bought. And it is not only the county history that survives him: «Hrvati i Karolinzi», the 2000 national exhibition catalogue of Croatia's Carolingian-period art, cites his 1932 and 1933 papers on the early-medieval church sculpture of Pula among its authorities — Gnirs, Marušić, Šonje, Rapanić, and De Franceschi.

name: Joso Defranceski
text: Author of «C. i kr. ratni logori 1914.-1918.» — the Imperial and Royal war camps, 1914–1918 — printed at Osijek. It is the early account of the Austro-Hungarian internment and refugee camps, the system that took thousands of Istrians to Wagna in Styria during the First World War, and it is still the source modern scholarship cites: the Rovigno centre's own monograph on Wagna lists it in its bibliography, and its 2015 reprint was launched at the Zvona i nari culture house at Ližnjan in Istria with the Centro di ricerche storiche present.
note: He spells the name exactly as this family does — Defranceski, fused, no particle. Nothing connects him to it. The National Union Catalog of pre-1956 imprints has the first edition.

name: Ivan Defranceski
text: Political commissar in the Istrian partisans. He was commissar of the II Company of the First Istrian Partisan Battalion, then of the battalion itself under the acting commander Vinko Brnčić, then of the II Pola Detachment in the Fifth Operational Zone, and finally of the First Partisan Detachment «Učka». At the founding parade of the Italian «Pino Budicin» battalion, in a village schoolroom between Sanvincenti and Gimino, he spoke in Croatian to about a hundred and twenty fighters, telling them to give everything for the ideals of justice and of national and social liberty for which Pino Budicin had died a few months before.
note: From «Rossa una stella», the Rovigno centre's monograph on the Budicin battalion (1975). The same fused spelling, in Istria, in the years this archive's own line was being moved to Germany. No connection is established.

name: Ante Defrančeški
text: A Croatian educationist of the new-school movement. He had three books out by 1934, among them «Načela nove škole» — Principles of the New School, Zagreb 1934 — and in 1939 he was one of the four editors of the «Pedagoški leksikon» published by Minerva at Zagreb, with Stevan Pataki, Marijan Tkalčić and Josip Demarin. He taught at a teachers' training school, and in 1932 he and his colleague Josip Škavić ran a Sokol gymnastics course at Crikvenica.
note: The Crikvenica detail is worth a second look rather than a claim. This archive's own line was living at Crikvenica from about 1890, and a man of the same rare fused surname was running a course there in 1932. It is a lead, not a link.

name: Josip Defranceski
text: A Yugoslav press official through the Cold War. A declassified American intelligence report on the Slav press in Argentina, dated 12 August 1947, names a Defranceski as director and editor of a Slav paper in Buenos Aires, «formerly connected with the Yugoslav Legation in Buenos Aires and considered pro-Tito». From 1954 to 1957 a Josip Defranceski appears in the United States State Department's Diplomatic List as Press Counselor of the Yugoslav embassy in Washington, with his addresses on 12th Street, Hamilton Street and Military Road. **And the middle of the career is now filled in.** The *Civil & Military Gazette* of Lahore, 5 December 1959, under the heading «Yugoslav Pressmen»: a delegation leaving Peshawar for **Kabul** on 14 December, consisting of «**Mr. Josip Defranceski, Director of External Services, Radio Belgrade**» and a correspondent of *Borba*. Buenos Aires in 1947, Washington from 1954 to 1957, **Radio Belgrade by 1959**, and still publishing in the Review of International Affairs in 1970.
note: Almost certainly one man across the whole run. Again the fused spelling, and again no established connection — but he was doing his work in Buenos Aires in the years the family in the French zone was being screened for Brazil.

name: Enrico de Franceschi
text:
**A baritone of La Scala**, and the British press of the 1920s and 30s puts him in the first rank. In June 1926 the *Illustrated London News*, *The Sketch* and *The Sphere* all carry the same advertisement listing the age's great voices — «Ansseau, Franz, **Martinelli** of the Metropolitan Opera House, Muratore (Tenors); **Amato, Galeffi, de Franceschi, Rouard, Stracciari** (Baritones); the star of stars, **La Jeritza**».

He recorded. *Gramophone, Wireless and Talking Machine News* reviews his duets with the soprano **Zita Fumagalli-Riva** in October and November 1924 — «Dite alla giovine» from *Traviata*, «O soave fanciulla» from *Bohème*, two duets from *Cavalleria rusticana* — and says simply: «**Here is very excellent singing.**» His solo disc of «O monumento» from *La Gioconda* and «Sei vendicata assai» from *Dinorah* was a ten-inch double-sided at two-and-six.

And on **8 March 1938** the BBC relayed *Lucia di Lammermoor* live **from La Scala, Milan** — orchestra under **Gino Marinuzzi**, chorus-master Vittore Veneziani, with **Enrico de Franceschi, Lina Pagliughi and Beniamino Gigli**. The listings ran in the *Yorkshire Evening Post* and the Portsmouth *Evening News*. A man of this name sang to Britain from La Scala, on the radio, seven months before Munich.

**And the Austrian press has him too — three hundred and ninety-two issues of it.** ANNO was searched properly on 13 September 2026 and the name clusters hard in **1930 and 1931**: Vienna above all, then **Salzburg, Klagenfurt, Linz, Eisenstadt** — *Die Stunde*, the *Illustrierte Kronen Zeitung*, the *Kärntner Zeitung*, the *Salzburger Chronik*, the *Wiener Zeitung*. He returns in 1934, with stray notices to 1944. Two Austrian seasons, on top of the Milan and London career already recorded here.
note: Found in the British newspaper archive, September 2026. No connection to any line on this site is claimed. He is here because he is the only person of the surname this archive has ever found whom the press simply called great. **He is also a warning.** He accounts for **two fifths of everything ANNO holds under this surname** — 392 issues of 950. Anyone searching the Austrian press for this family will hit him first, repeatedly, and should know at once that he is not ours. **And he is not the other Enrico.** This archive also holds an *«Enrico de Franceschi»* in the «Guida schematica di Trieste» of **1869**, named as the man behind the merchant house *«Gleyre Costante (Enrico de Franceschi), in manifatture e pece»* — textiles and pitch, at Via S. Spiridione 7. Fifty-five years and a different trade separate them, and no attempt has been made to connect the two. **Two men, one name, one coast** — which on this surname is the normal condition and not a puzzle.

name: Don Nicolò de Franceschi, canon of Candia
text:
Found in the burial register of the cathedral parish of St Domnius at Split, September 2026, and previously known to this archive only as an index line reading «Nicolo De Franceschi, burial 18 May 1716».

«**Can.co Don Nicolò de Franceschi**, ⟨*Can.co di S. Vito di Candia*⟩, passò da questa alla miglior vita **d'anni 90 incirca** … et **fù sepolto nella Chiesa del Domo in Coro nella sepoltura delli Sig.ri Can.ci**.»

**A canon of a church in Candia — Crete — buried in the choir of Split cathedral, in the canons' vault, at about ninety.** Ninety in 1716 puts his birth about **1626**; **Candia fell to the Ottomans in 1669**, when he was forty-three. He held the title of a chapter that the Turks had taken.
note: The register writes «S. Vito»; the great church of Candia was San Tito, and a clerk at Split could readily set one for the other. He is the first documented link between the Cretan De Franceschi — the branch the Seget family claims — and Dalmatia. No descent is claimed here. See Seget.

name: Antun Defranceski, accounting councillor
text:
**The name inside the Zagreb government, and attached to nothing here.**

*«Narodne novine», **8 June 1863**, printing the royal appointments: «Računarskim savjetnikom: pregledalac računah **Antun Defranceski**» — **appointed accounting councillor**, promoted from inspector of accounts.*

*«Domobran», **17 January 1865**: a subscription got up for the singing studies of a Miss Ema Vizjak in Milan, and among those giving a florin each are «Maurović, Kučenjak, **Defranceschi** i Jugović, **činovnici kr. građ. ravnateljstva**» — **officials of the royal building directorate**.*

**He is here because a one-name study records the name where it falls.** *He is in **Zagreb**, not Istria and not the Kvarner; **nothing joins him to any line on this site**; and the spelling «Defranceski» is this family's own — **which is why he needs saying out loud rather than filing quietly**. A civil servant with a dated promotion leaves a paper trail, and the Croatian State Archives hold the personnel files that would place him.*
note: *The 1865 entry gives no forename, so that the two are one man is **inf**. Found 28 September 2026 on the Portal Stare hrvatske novine. © Portal Stare hrvatske novine, Nacionalna i sveučilišna knjižnica u Zagrebu, 2009.*

name: Peter Simon Defranceschi, surgeon
text:
Born **26 October 1863 at Ajdovščina** in the Vipava valley, the son of **Filip Defranceschi, a merchant**, and **Jožefa Kalin**, who died of consumption when he was barely four. Put out of the gymnasium at Novo mesto for belonging to an illegal national society, he matured at Gorizia in 1885, took his medical degree at Graz in 1890, worked under Wölfler at Graz and, in 1893, under Chrobak at Vienna. From **1894 he was district physician at Novo mesto and head surgeon of the Brothers of Mercy hospital at Kandija**, and fought six years for the women's hospital there, opened in November 1908; he moved to Gorizia in 1910 (chief surgeon from 1915), spent the war at Graz and Vienna, and in 1918 was the Yugoslav government's first attaché at Vienna. He wrote from 1898 on forensic medicine, among the first in Slovene. **A street beside the women's hospital at Novo mesto is named after him.** He married **Dionysia Dolžan** (born at **Pazin**, 1881) at Graz on 24 November 1900; their daughter Adalberta was born at Novo mesto in 1902.

**His sister Emma, schoolmistress at Kastav,** married the municipal surveyor **Ferdinand Kleinmayer on 12 March 1893** (Kastav marriage book, image 101, read here at level 13: she «Emma Defranceschi, Magistra Scholae», 31, of «Sugulj 83»; her parents «defuncti Philippus Defranceschi, possessor» and «Josepha Kalin»; *doc*). A WikiTree profile (*lore*) gives her as born at Ajdovščina on 9 November 1861, died at Ljubljana on 13 December 1912, and has a second sister, Karolina (b. 1859). Their mother's death about 1867 is in the biography, not in the 1893 entry. Their father is **Filip** in Slovene, **Philippus** in the Latin of the Kastav book.

**What the registers say (9 November 2026, read in the Matricula viewer, *doc*).** The Graz marriage book gives the groom as «Dr. Peter Defranceschi, Primararzt», born at «Haidenschaft im Küstenlande» (Ajdovščina), son of the late merchant «Philipp Defranceschi» and «Maria geb. Kalin» — the mother is *Maria* here and *Josepha* at Kastav in 1893, a difference not yet settled. His wife is «geb. von Pisino» (Pazin). The Ljubljana death book has his sister **Emma, «pl. Kleinmayer, geometrova žena», born at Ajdovščina on 9 November 1861, dead 13 December 1912** of cancer of the breast.

**His wife's baptism (Pazin, read 9 November 2026, *doc*).** Dionysia Maria Anna Dolžan was baptised at Pazin on **11 September 1881**, born the 2nd, the daughter of «Josephus Dolzan, telegraphista» and «Albertha Bernat» (house 98; godparents Giov. and Maria Scarpa, a telegraph inspector and his wife); the Pazin baptism book (1847–1882, FamilySearch 9R26-168, image 189, folio 472) agrees with the Graz marriage on the date and the parents, writes the mother's first name Albertha where Graz has Albertina and the index Ada, and carries a later note of her death at Ljubljana on 26 September 1962. A telegraph official's daughter, probably born at Pazin on a posting (*inf*); nothing in it touches a Pazin Defranceschi.

**Her father was at Pazin by 1878 (read 10 November 2026, *doc*).** «Josephus Dolžan, k.k. Telegraphenbeamter» stands godfather in the Pazin baptism book on **14 November 1878** (house 162, image 171, folio 438; level 13), three years before Dionysia's baptism there, so the birth is a posting of some years and not a visit (*inf*). The sweep of the whole book (1847–1882) finds him in no other entry, and no other child of his.
note: **Not shown to be kin.** The name is the same name. No document in this archive joins the Vipava-valley Defranceschi — Filip (b. about 1828), his father **Peter** (about 1800) and a mother Marija Repič, as WikiTree gives them — to any of the seven stocks. **One thing coincides and is only that:** [«Johann Defranceski von Sturja»](/imperial/), a court-appointed curator in the Laibach gazette from 1865 to 1875; Šturje is part of Ajdovščina, so he lived in the same town and the same years as Filip; nothing says whether they were kin. *Sources:* Slovenski biografski leksikon (1925) and Primorski slovenski biografski leksikon (1977), [Slovenska biografija](https://www.slovenska-biografija.si/oseba/sbi170986/); Slovene Wikipedia; WikiTree profiles Defranceschi-11, -16, -17, -18, -19, Kalin-296, Kalin-297, Dolžan-13 (a single contributor's tree; **the Graz marriage page (entry 244, 24 November 1900) and the Ljubljana death page (entry 372, 13 December 1912) were opened and read here on 9 November 2026 and agree with it; the Ajdovščina baptism images are shown by Matricula's viewer as «blocked for legal reasons or not found» and are not read**); the Kastav marriage book of 1884–1904, waypoint 9R2Z-ZNL, told on [the Kalanj page](/kalanj/); the Pazin baptism book 1847–1882, waypoint 9R26-168, image 189.

name: Simon de Franceschi, seigneur de Rougemont
text: Said by a French family-history blog to have come from Florence (the blog adds a query), naturalised and ennobled by letters patent of **9 February 1611**, lord of the château of Rougemont near Châteaudun from 1596, squire to Louis XIII and Master of Waters and Forests of the county of Dunois in 1620. He married **Anne Chouaine** in 1595, died on **15 January 1631** and was buried in the church of Saint-Jean-Froidmentel; they left three children, a daughter and two sons, and the line is followed in the blog and in David's MyHeritage tree into the seventeenth century. **The departmental archives of Loir-et-Cher, where the château lies, give a different year and a different king's wife: the purchase is of 28 January 1597, and in 1610 he is gentilhomme-servant of the Queen, Marie de Médicis (22 November 2026, below).**
note: `lore` except where marked `doc` at the end: the blog (franceschi.centerblog.net) and the tree are the main sources, and no register has been read here (what is marked `doc` is a finding-aid abstract, not the act). **No kinship to the Istrian, Kvarner or Carnian Defranceschi is claimed.** The same GEDCOM runs on into a Corsican and Genoese branch of the name (Bastia, Aachen, Danzig, 1727–1915), told in the same way on these people's pages; the tree also hangs this Simon on a nameless placeholder father with five unrelated people of the name under him, which is a MyHeritage artefact and is not drawn. The people are in the [roster](/people/) and the households with a namesake line. **First records, 18 Nov 2026** (finding-aid abstracts in FranceArchives, `doc` for what they say, acts not seen): the family is in the Paris notarial and Châtelet records from 1633 as «de Franceschy» or «de Franceschi, chevalier, sieur de Rougemont», **Charles**, gentilhomme ordinaire de la chambre du Roi, of the château of Rougemont in Saint-Jean-Froidmentel; his marriage contract with Catherine Briant, widow of Antoine Clémenceau, is of 1636 (not the blog's «avant 1623», and not the blog's Michel Pagot); his son **Pierre-Charles** is lord of Rougemont and husband of **Françoise Chevalier**, daughter of the baron of Monthyon (Archives départementales de Seine-et-Marne, E64); and the widow of the other branch's lord of La Renoullière, Anne de Turin, is married to a Piedefer by 1677, her first husband called Jean, not Simon, in that abstract. No record of Simon senior or of the 1595 marriage was found. The search was the FranceArchives portal under «de franceschi» (all 34 pages, 1,672 hits, 36 dated before 1800), «franceschy» and «francesche»; the departmental archives of Loir-et-Cher, where Rougemont lies, are not in that portal's hits; their printed inventory is read below, and their digital archive is the next place to write to. **Archives nationales, virtual reading room (SIV), 18 Nov 2026** (finding-aid abstracts again, `doc` for what they say; the acts not seen): the SIV's own search, run on «francischy», «franceschy», «francesche», «rougemont franceschi» and «franceschi dunois», gives the set FranceArchives gave and **one entry the portal did not show**: Châtelet de Paris, insinuations, Y//183, fol. 144, act of **16 August 1643** ([the notice](https://www.siv.archives-nationales.culture.gouv.fr/siv/rechercheconsultation/consultation/ir/consultationIR.action?irId=FRAN_IR_005819&udId=d_3_305&details=true)), in which «Charles de Francischy, chevalier, seigneur de Rougemont, gentilhomme ordinaire de la chambre du Roi», of the château of Rougemont in Saint-Jean-Froidmentel, county of Dunois, then lodging in the rue de la Truanderie, parish of Saint-Eustache, gives a life annuity of 150 livres tournois to **Simon Repérant**, conseiller secrétaire du Roi, and Marguerite de Neufbourg, his wife, whom he calls his cousin and cousine. «Francischy» is a spelling new to the set. The power of attorney of 12 March 1659 (Pièce n°38) has its own [SIV notice](https://www.siv.archives-nationales.culture.gouv.fr/siv/rechercheconsultation/consultation/ir/consultationIR.action?irId=FRAN_IR_001382&udId=d_1_1_19_33&details=true). The SIV search for «chouaine» and «chouayne» gives Paris and Chartres acts that name the family of Anne Chouaine: leads only, none read. **Archives de Loir-et-Cher, 22 Nov 2026** (`doc` for what a printed summary says; the acts not seen). Rougemont and Saint-Jean-Froidmentel are in **Loir-et-Cher**, not Eure-et-Loir: Châteaudun was only the seat of the Dunois. Two printed summaries of the estate's papers (series E 153-180), read in the archive.org copies. (1) The *Bulletin de la Société archéologique, scientifique et littéraire du Vendômois*, vol. 35 (1896), pp. 106-108, says that on **28 January 1597** «noble homme Simon Francisque (ou Franceschi), sieur de Vimoy», a small fief beside Rougemont, bought the château from the heirs of Henri de Fors; that in **1610** he took the title of gentilhomme-servant of the Queen (Marie de Médicis) and in **1620** that of Master of Waters and Forests of the county of Dunois (the blog's 1620 stands); that the château was built from about 1610, not 1597; and that in **1678** Charles de Franceschi was still lord of Rougemont and in **1684** his widow **Françoise Chevalier**, then wife of Éléonor Courtin, lord of Molléans, still held it. (2) The printed *Inventaire sommaire des Archives départementales antérieures à 1790, Loir-et-Cher* (Blois, 1887), pp. 37-40: E 153, the cession of the lands of Bois-Garnier and Rougemont by the Béthunes to «Simon Francisque de Vimoy»; E 161, a sentence against «Charles de Francesky, seigneur de Rougemont» and the forced sale of 1687 from «Françoise Chevalier, veuve de Charles de Francesky» to the Desmé de la Chesnaye; E 163 and E 164, receipts to «Charles de Franceschi, chevalier, seigneur de Rougemont» and the inventory of titles found in the château in 1686. **What it changes:** the blog's «1596» is 1597 in the archives; and Françoise Chevalier is called the widow of **Charles**, where the Seine-et-Marne abstract makes her the wife of Pierre-Charles, so whether the Charles of 1636 (wife Catherine Briant) and the lord of 1678 are one man is open (inf). Spellings new to this archive: **Francesky** (E 161) and **Francisque** (E 153 and the Bulletin; also a given name); neither is claimed for the Istrian family. Not read: the acts, the Saint-Jean-Froidmentel registers, the digital finding aid (the departmental site's bot check was not worked round).

name: Marco de Franceschi
text: Bishop of Cefalonia e Zante (Kephalonia and Zakynthos, in the Ionian Sea) from 29 July 1488 until his death in 1521; Eubel's third volume lists the see vacant «ob. Marci» before Ferdinando de' Medici was provided. Nothing else is known here: no birthplace, no family, no document of his own. Zante is also a stop on the Candia → Zante → Šibenik road of the Seget family's account (see Seget); the two are not linked, and no descent is claimed.
note: Catholic-Hierarchy (bishop/bfrancem), citing Gams, Series episcoporum, p. 48; Eubel, Hierarchia catholica III, Cephalonia and Zante (the vacancy «ob. Marci»). His own 1488 entry in Eubel II was not found in the scan's text.
